documents.title: Guided Notes: Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Mass
documents.directions: Fill in each blank as we go. Use the word bank only if you get stuck.

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 1: Atoms are rearranged
sections.directions: Word bank: rearranged · created · destroyed · after · somewhere

questions.prompt: In a chemical reaction, atoms are ______________ into new substances.
questions.why: Atoms trade partners to make new substances.

questions.prompt: No atoms are ______________ and none are ______________.
questions.why: Either order of the two words is fine: "created ... destroyed" or "destroyed ... created".

questions.prompt: So the total mass before a reaction equals the total mass ______________ it.
questions.why: Same atoms before and after, so the same mass.

questions.prompt: When it looks like mass changed, the atoms went ______________: something got in or got out (usually a gas).
questions.why: Mr. Okafor's rule: we say "the atoms went somewhere."

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: A friend says, "When the candle burned, some of the mass just disappeared." How would you fix that sentence? Use the word atoms.
questions.answer: The atoms did not disappear; they went somewhere. They joined into new substances, like gases that went into the air, so the mass is still there, just not on the table.
questions.why: Look for: atoms named, the idea that they went somewhere (into the air as gas), never "the mass disappeared."

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 2: Reactants and products
sections.directions: Word bank: reactants · products · left · right · yields

questions.prompt: ______________ are the substances you start with.
questions.why: Reactants go in.

questions.prompt: They are written on the ______________ side of a chemical equation.
questions.why: "Left is what we start with."

questions.prompt: ______________ are the new substances that form. They are written on the ______________ side.
questions.why: Products come out, on the right of the arrow.

questions.prompt: The arrow (→) means "react to form" or "______________."
questions.why: A plus sign separates two reactants or two products.

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, name the reactants and the product. How do you know which is which?
questions.answer: Reactants: H₂ (hydrogen) and O₂ (oxygen). Product: H₂O (water). The reactants are on the left of the arrow and the product is on the right.
questions.why: Look for: H₂ and O₂ as reactants, H₂O as the product, and "left / right of the arrow" as the reason.

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 3: Signs of a chemical change
sections.directions: Word bank: new · precipitate · color · temperature · proof · physical

questions.prompt: A chemical change makes a ______________ substance.
questions.why: That is the test for every example: is there a new substance?

questions.prompt: A solid that forms when two clear liquids are mixed is called a ______________.
questions.why: Clue 2 on the list.

questions.prompt: Other clues: a gas forms, an unexpected ______________ change, a ______________ change without outside heating or cooling, or light or a new odor.
questions.why: The five clues: gas, precipitate, color, temperature, light or odor.

questions.prompt: One clue alone is not ______________.
questions.why: Bubbles from boiling water are a clue, but no new substance forms.

questions.prompt: Boiling water, melting ice and crushing a can are ______________ changes, because no new substance forms.
questions.why: Changes of state and changes of shape are physical.

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: Water boiling on the stove makes bubbles. Is it a chemical change? Explain.
questions.answer: No. It is a physical change (a change of state). The bubbles are still water, just as a gas; no new substance forms.
questions.why: Look for: "physical", "no new substance", and that bubbles alone are not proof.

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 4: Reading a formula and counting atoms
sections.directions: Word bank: subscript · coefficient · one · everything · table

questions.prompt: The ______________ is the small number after a symbol. It tells how many atoms of that element are in one molecule.
questions.why: H₂O: the small 2 means 2 hydrogen atoms.

questions.prompt: No subscript means ______________ atom.
questions.why: The O in H₂O has no subscript, so there is 1 oxygen atom.

questions.prompt: The ______________ is the big number in front. It tells how many molecules.
questions.why: 3H₂O means 3 molecules of water.

questions.prompt: In Ca(OH)₂, the 2 after the parentheses applies to ______________ inside them.
questions.why: Ca(OH)₂: 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H.

questions.prompt: We always count atoms with a ______________: element, reactant side, product side.
questions.why: Mr. Okafor's counting table.

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: Fill in the counting table for 3H₂O (just this one formula, in the "Reactant side" column). Show the multiplying.
questions.answer: H: 3 × 2 = 6 hydrogen atoms. O: 3 × 1 = 3 oxygen atoms.
questions.why: Look for: coefficient times subscript for each element; 6 H and 3 O.

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 5: Balancing simple equations
sections.directions: Word bank: same · coefficients · subscript · recount · conservation

questions.prompt: A balanced equation has the ______________ number of atoms of each element on both sides.
questions.why: Atoms, not molecules: every row of the table matches.

questions.prompt: A balanced equation is ______________ of mass written in symbols.
questions.why: Same atoms on both sides means the same mass.

questions.prompt: Balance by changing ______________ only.
questions.why: Coefficients change how many molecules, not what the substance is.

questions.prompt: Never change a ______________: that changes the substance (H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, not water).
questions.why: The most common balancing mistake.

questions.prompt: Steps: count atoms in a table → pick an element that doesn't match → change a coefficient → ______________ everything → repeat until every row matches.
questions.why: Changing one coefficient can change more than one row, so recount all of them.

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: Balance N₂ + H₂ → NH₃ by writing coefficients. Use the counting table to check it.
questions.answer: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. N: 2 on the reactant side, 2 on the product side. H: 6 on the reactant side, 6 on the product side.
questions.why: Look for: coefficients only (no subscripts changed), 1, 3, 2, and a table where both rows match.

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 6: Closed and open systems
sections.directions: Word bank: closed · open · escape · more · same

questions.prompt: A ______________ system lets nothing in or out, like a sealed flask or a zip bag.
questions.why: Nothing in, nothing out: the balance reading stays the same.

questions.prompt: In a closed system, the mass on the balance stays the ______________ before and after the reaction.
questions.why: Zip bag lab: 150.0 g before, 150.0 g after.

questions.prompt: An ______________ system lets matter in or out, like an open cup.
questions.why: Gas can leave, or a gas from the air can join in.

questions.prompt: In an open cup, a gas product can ______________, so the balance shows less mass after.
questions.why: Open cup lab: the CO₂ gas left the cup.

questions.prompt: When steel wool burns on a balance, iron atoms join with oxygen atoms from the air. The balance shows ______________ mass after the burning than before.
questions.why: Mass of steel wool + mass of oxygen used = mass of the iron oxide made.

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: Baking soda and vinegar in an open cup: 150.0 g before, 148.9 g after. What mass of gas escaped, and where did it go?
questions.answer: 150.0 g − 148.9 g = 1.1 g of carbon dioxide gas. It left the cup and went into the air. The atoms went somewhere; the mass did not disappear.
questions.why: Look for: 1.1 g, CO₂ (a gas) leaving the open cup, and gas having mass.

documents.title: Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Mass
documents.notes: Ask: "If you burn a piece of paper, where does it go?" Take three answers and write them on the board without judging. We come back to them at the end. Today's goal: be able to say where the atoms went.

slides.title: Big idea: atoms are rearranged
bullets: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms into new substances
No atoms are created and none are destroyed
Total mass before = total mass after
If the mass seems to change, something got in or got out (usually a gas)
slides.notes: Ask: "If no atoms are made or lost, what should happen to the mass?" Push for "it stays the same." Then ask: "So when a balance shows a different number, what must have happened?" Listen for "something got in or out." Model the sentence: "The atoms went somewhere." Correct any "the mass disappeared" on the spot.

slides.title: Reactants and products
bullets: Reactants: what you start with (left side)
Products: the new substances that form (right side)
The arrow → means "react to form" or "yields"
A plus sign separates two reactants or two products
Board example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
slides.notes: Point at 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Ask: "Which side is what we start with?" (left). "Name the reactants." (H₂ and O₂.) "Name the product." (H₂O.) Then say it in words: "Hydrogen gas and oxygen gas react to form water," and ask a student to point to each substance. Students mix these up in word equations, so have the class say "left is what we start with" together.

slides.title: Signs of a chemical change
bullets: A chemical change makes a new substance
Clues: a new gas (bubbles), a precipitate, an unexpected color change, a temperature change on its own, light or a new odor
One clue alone is not proof
Physical changes: ice melting, sugar dissolving, cutting paper, crushing a can
Chemical changes: rusting iron, baking a cake, burning wood, a glow stick lighting up
slides.notes: Ask: "Boiling water makes bubbles. Is that a chemical change?" Let them argue, then ask: "Is there a new substance?" (No, it is still water: a change of state.) Then go down the lists: "Thumbs up for chemical, thumbs down for physical: sugar dissolving... a glow stick lighting up..." Ask a student to name which clue a glow stick shows (light).

slides.title: Reading a formula and counting atoms
bullets: Subscript (small number after a symbol): atoms of that element in one molecule
No subscript means 1
Coefficient (big number in front): how many molecules
Parentheses: Ca(OH)₂ has 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H
Always count with the table
slides.notes: Write H₂O and ask: "How many hydrogen atoms? How many oxygen?" (2 and 1.) Then write 3H₂O and ask: "Now how many of each?" Have them fill in the table on their notes before you show 6 H and 3 O. Then ask: "In Ca(OH)₂, what does the 2 apply to?" (everything inside the parentheses).

slides.title: Balancing simple equations
bullets: Balanced: the same number of atoms of each element on both sides
That is conservation of mass in symbols
Change coefficients only, never subscripts
Steps: table → find a row that doesn't match → change a coefficient → recount everything → repeat
Practice: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, challenge: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃
slides.notes: Start with H₂ + O₂ → H₂O unbalanced. Ask: "Which row of the table doesn't match?" (O.) "Someone wants to write H₂O₂. Why can't we?" (That is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance.) Then ask: "2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O has 3 molecules on the left and 2 on the right. Is it balanced?" (Yes: count atoms, not molecules.) Watch for anyone writing a 2 as a subscript and catch it every time.

slides.title: Closed vs. open systems
bullets: Closed system: nothing gets in or out (sealed flask, zip bag, balloon over a bottle); the mass stays the same
Open system: matter can get in or out (open cup or beaker)
A gas product can escape, so the balance can show less
A gas from the air can join a product, so the balance can show more
Steel wool burning gets heavier: iron joins with oxygen from the air
slides.notes: Ask: "In our lab, the zip bag puffed up. What is inside it?" (The CO₂ gas.) "Why did the open cup lose mass but the bag didn't?" (The gas left the cup; it was trapped in the bag.) Then ask: "Steel wool gets heavier when it burns. Where did the extra mass come from?" (Oxygen atoms from the air.) Ask a student to say the steel wool sentence: steel wool + oxygen used = iron oxide made.

slides.title: Closed vs. open flask
bullets: Both flasks start at the same mass and hold the same reaction, which makes a gas
Flask 1 is open; Flask 2 has a balloon stretched over the top
Predict each balance reading after the reaction
Explain where the gas went in each flask
slides.notes: Ask: "Predict: after the reaction, will Flask 1 read more, less or the same? Flask 2?" Have them write the prediction first, then share with a partner. Ask: "What will the balloon on Flask 2 do?" (Puff up, because the gas is trapped.) Then: "How could we find the mass of the gas that left Flask 1?" (mass before − mass after). Listen for "the gas went into the air," and correct "the gas has no mass" right away: gas has mass.

slides.title: Mass problems
bullets: Mass of reactants = mass of products
10.0 g of A + 6.0 g of B, one product: 16.0 g of product
Gas escaping an open container: mass of gas = mass before − mass after
We measure mass in grams on a balance (mass, not weight)
slides.notes: Ask: "If 10.0 g of A reacts with 6.0 g of B and only one product forms, how much product?" (16.0 g.) Then: "In the open cup, 150.0 g became 148.9 g. How much CO₂ left?" (1.1 g.) Ask: "What do we measure on a balance: mass or weight?" (Mass, in grams.) Close by going back to the paper question from the start: "Where did the burned paper go?"

slides.title: Watch out for these mistakes
bullets: "The mass disappeared": no, the atoms went somewhere. Gas has mass.
Changing a subscript to balance changes the substance
Balanced means the same atoms on each side, not the same number of molecules
Not all bubbles mean a chemical change
In this unit we say mass, measured in grams
slides.notes: Read each mistake and ask: "What would you say to a friend who wrote this?" Call on a different student for each one. For the molecules one, ask: "2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: 3 molecules become 2. Balanced or not? Prove it with the table."

documents.title: Chemical Reactions Quiz
documents.directions: Read each question all the way through. Circle the letter of the best answer. For the last part, write in complete sentences.

prompt.A: In the equation CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, which substances are the products?
prompt.B: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Which list names the reactants?

why.A: Products are the new substances, written on the right of the arrow: CO₂ and H₂O.
why.B: Reactants are what you start with: magnesium and oxygen. Magnesium oxide is the product.

prompt.A: In 3H₂O, what does the 3 tell you?
prompt.B: In CO₂, what does the small 2 tell you?

A: The water has a mass of 3 grams.
B: There are 2 molecules of carbon dioxide in all.
The carbon atom is counted two times.

why.A: The big number in front is a coefficient: it tells how many molecules (3 water molecules).
why.B: The small number after a symbol is a subscript: 2 oxygen atoms in one molecule of CO₂.

prompt.A: Which of these is a chemical change?
prompt.B: Which of these is a physical change?

B: A cake baking in the oven

why.A: A glow stick gives off light because a new substance forms. Melting, dissolving and crushing make no new substance.
why.B: Cutting paper only changes its shape; it is still paper. Rusting, baking and burning make new substances.

prompt.A: Use the counting table. How many atoms of each element are in 2Ca(OH)₂? Each answer lists Ca, O, H in that order.
prompt.B: Use the counting table. How many atoms of each element are in 2Fe₂O₃? Each answer lists Fe, O in that order.

why.A: The coefficient 2 multiplies everything: Ca 2 × 1 = 2; the parentheses hold O and H, each 2 × 2 = 4.

prompt.B: Which equation for rust is balanced?

why.A: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO: Mg 2 and 2, O 2 and 2. Every row of the table matches.
why.B: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃: Fe 4 and 4, O 6 and 6. Every row of the table matches.

prompt.A: In a sealed flask, 12.0 g of substance A reacts with 5.0 g of substance B. Only one product forms. What is the mass of the product, in grams?
prompt.B: In a sealed zip bag, 25.0 g of substance C reacts with 9.5 g of substance D. Only one product forms. What is the mass of the product, in grams?

why.A: Mass of reactants = mass of products: 12.0 g + 5.0 g = 17.0 g.
why.B: Mass of reactants = mass of products: 25.0 g + 9.5 g = 34.5 g.

why.A: Open system: the CO₂ gas escapes into the air, so the reading drops below 150.0 g. A balloon over the cup traps the gas (a closed system), so the after reading stays 150.0 g. The atoms went somewhere; gas has mass.
why.B: Closed system: the CO₂ is trapped in the bag (that is why it puffs up), so the reading stays 150.0 g. Leaving the bag open lets the gas escape into the air, so the after reading would be lower. Gas has mass.

prompt.A: Dev starts balancing Al + Cl₂ → AlCl₃ by writing a 2 in front of AlCl₃. He counts atoms and finds two rows that still don't match. Which change correctly finishes balancing it?
prompt.B: Rosa starts balancing Fe + Cl₂ → FeCl₃ by writing a 2 in front of Fe. She counts atoms and finds two rows that still don't match. Which change correctly finishes balancing it?

A: Put a 2 before Al, then rewrite Cl₂ as Cl₆
Write a 2 before Al and a 3 before Cl₂
Write a 3 before Cl₂ but leave Al alone
Write 6 in front of Cl₂, then a 2 before Al
B: Give Cl₂ a 3 and leave FeCl₃ as it is
Turn FeCl₃ into Fe₂Cl₂ so both sides have 2 Fe and 2 Cl
Write 3FeCl₃ on the right and 2Cl₂ on the left
Use 3Cl₂ on the left and 2FeCl₃ on the right

why.A: After the 2 on AlCl₃: Al 1 on the left, 2 on the right; Cl 2 on the left, 6 on the right. Two coefficients are needed: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃ gives Al 2 and 2, Cl 3 × 2 = 6 and 2 × 3 = 6. A 2 before Al with Cl₂ rewritten as Cl₆ makes the counts match (Al 2 and 2, Cl 6 and 6) but changes a subscript, so it is no longer chlorine gas. A 3 before Cl₂ alone fixes Cl (6 and 6) but leaves Al unmatched (1 vs 2). A 6 before Cl₂ puts 12 Cl on the left against 6 on the right: the 6 is the count of Cl atoms needed, not the number of Cl₂ molecules.
why.B: After the 2 on Fe: Fe 2 on the left, 1 on the right; Cl 2 on the left, 3 on the right. Two coefficients are needed: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃ gives Fe 2 and 2, Cl 3 × 2 = 6 and 2 × 3 = 6. A 3 on Cl₂ with no coefficient on FeCl₃ leaves Fe at 2 vs 1 and Cl at 6 vs 3. Turning FeCl₃ into Fe₂Cl₂ makes the counts match but changes subscripts, so it is a different substance. Swapping the numbers (3FeCl₃ and 2Cl₂) gives Fe 2 vs 3 and Cl 4 vs 9.

prompt.A: A class does the baking soda and vinegar lab in an open cup. The balance reads 120.0 g before and 118.6 g after. (a) What mass of gas left the cup? (b) Explain why the same reaction in a sealed zip bag would read 120.0 g after. Use the words mass and gas.
prompt.B: A pad of steel wool on a balance reads 5.0 g. It burns in open air, and afterward the balance reads 6.2 g. (a) What mass of oxygen joined the iron? (b) Kayla says the extra mass was created by the fire. Explain why she is wrong. Use the words mass and atoms.

answer.A: (a) 120.0 g − 118.6 g = 1.4 g of carbon dioxide gas. (b) In the open cup the gas escaped into the air, so the balance no longer measured its mass; the 1.4 g of gas is now in the air. In a sealed bag the gas is trapped, so all of the mass stays on the balance and it reads 120.0 g.
answer.B: (a) 6.2 g − 5.0 g = 1.2 g of oxygen. (b) No mass was created. Iron atoms joined with oxygen atoms from the air, and those oxygen atoms have mass, so the iron oxide has more mass than the steel wool: 5.0 g of steel wool + 1.2 g of oxygen = 6.2 g of iron oxide.

why.A: Look for: 1.4 g; the gas left the open cup; the gas has mass and stays in the closed bag. A full answer never says the mass disappeared.
why.B: Look for: 1.2 g; oxygen atoms from the air joined the iron; atoms are not created. Steel wool + oxygen used = iron oxide made.

prompt.A: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O has 3 molecules on the reactant side and 2 on the product side. Marcus says it can't be balanced. Is he right? Use a counting table to explain.
prompt.B: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ has 4 molecules on the reactant side and 2 on the product side. Lena says it can't be balanced. Is she right? Use a counting table to explain.

answer.A: No. Balanced means the same number of atoms of each element, not the same number of molecules. H: 4 on the reactant side, 4 on the product side. O: 2 and 2. Every row matches, so it is balanced.
answer.B: No. Balanced means the same number of atoms of each element, not the same number of molecules. N: 2 on the reactant side, 2 on the product side. H: 6 and 6. Every row matches, so it is balanced.

why.A: Look for: "No", a table with H 4/4 and O 2/2, and atoms (not molecules) as the reason.
why.B: Look for: "No", a table with N 2/2 and H 6/6, and atoms (not molecules) as the reason.
